first.rationale: Two inherited beliefs are both decision-critical this week and measured against the wrong objective. memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the most tempting response to the competitor's entry pricing and would be the largest, hardest-to-reverse commitment, yet its recorded support is 'acquisition and revenue lift' — short-horizon top-line, with nothing about margin durability, retention of discount-acquired SMBs, or whether that revenue stays qualified. Under a sustainable long-term qualified revenue objective that is exactly the kind of under-supported, high-consequence claim triage says to pull. memory_31 is my second pull because it directly underwrites the direction I currently intend: cutting required signup fields lifted first-week activation, but activation is a proxy, and removing qualifying fields is a classic way to buy activation with lead quality — the lift may be real and still hostile to qualified revenue downstream. I want the original record to see whether revenue/quality was tracked or only the activation proxy. I deliberately did not spend the budget on memory_86 (same direction, and verifying memory_31 tests the riskier mechanism), memory_57 (referral needs an established base, doesn't address the SMB activation/onboarding decline), memory_91 (cheap, low-blast-radius, and consistent with the funnel diagnosis), or memory_44 (enterprise, off-target for the SMB pressure driving this quarter). Current intent: attack the funnel, not the price. Both failing metrics — onboarding completion -4%, activation -6% — sit in the same stretch of the funnel, so simplify_onboarding addresses the actual observed regression rather than discounting against a competitor's terms. I run it as a small guarded test, not a broad rollout: the inherited evidence is 24-52 days old, predates the competitor's entry, and is denominated in activation rather than qualified revenue. Guardrails must include lead-quality and downstream conversion metrics, not just completion rate, precisely because the field-cutting mechanism can inflate the proxy while degrading the objective. If memory_31's archive shows quality was never measured, I keep the test but shrink it further and instrument for qualified conversion; if memory_73's archive shows durable retained margin rather than a one-quarter acquisition spike, promotional_pricing becomes a live contender and I would reconsider before committing the slot.

final.rationale:
Both pulls paid off, and in opposite directions. memory_73 was actively misleading as consolidated: exp_73 shows signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% but 30-day retention -12%, and the original record explicitly concludes the discounted cohort does not survive first renewal and that targeted discounting must NOT be generalized as a sustainable-growth strategy. The inherited summary had laundered a warning into an endorsement by keeping the top-line numbers and dropping the retention collapse. Against a sustainable long-term qualified revenue objective, promotional_pricing is now disqualified — it would have bought back the competitor's SMB accounts with revenue that churns out inside a quarter, and matching entry pricing under competitive pressure is precisely when that failure mode is most tempting and most expensive. I am treating the competitor's pricing as a condition to out-execute on time-to-value, not to match on price.

memory_31 verified clean and, importantly, verified on the right denominator: signup +15%, activation +9%, retention -1%, qualified revenue +4%. My prior worry was that cutting required fields buys the activation proxy at the cost of lead quality; the source record tracked qualified revenue and retention directly and both held. That converts my intended direction from proxy-supported to objective-supported, so I move from small_guarded_test to standard_experiment.

I do not go broader than that. exp_31's conclusion states it holds on SMB and was not replicated on other segments, so I scope the experiment to SMB self-serve and do not extend it to enterprise — memory_44's sales-assisted demo path stays intact for enterprise, since a self-serve simplification there would cut against the flow that produces pipeline quality. Two further sources of uncertainty remain unretired: memory_86 and memory_91 were never pulled, so the broader onboarding-shortening and activation-messaging claims are still only as good as their consolidated summaries, and memory_73 proves those summaries can invert the original finding. I am relying on memory_86/memory_91 only as weak directional support for attacking the funnel, not as load-bearing evidence. The evidence is also 45-64 days old and predates the competitor's entry, so the acquired mix may differ from exp_31's cohort.

Decision: run signup/onboarding simplification on SMB this week as a controlled experiment with a holdout. Primary metric is qualified revenue and 30-day retention, not completion or activation rate; completion and activation are diagnostic only. Explicit kill condition: if retention degrades beyond the roughly -1% seen in exp_31, or if the incremental cohort's qualified conversion runs below the control, stop rather than scale — that is the exp_73 signature appearing in a different wrapper. I am also flagging that memory_73 should be corrected in durable memory so the next session does not inherit the same inverted claim.
